title: With hardship, ease
hookLine: with every hardship comes ease, said twice

lines: SAID AGAIN, ALMOST WORD FOR WORD.
cards: "But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease." That's Marmaduke Pickthall's English for two short verses of the Quran. Read it slowly and something odd happens.
Apart from the 'but' that opens the first, the second line is the same words in the same order. In an essay, you'd cut it.
And there it is, said again, the way you'd say something twice to a friend who didn't quite hear you. Or didn't quite believe it.

teach.b: First, the chapter. It's one of the short ones near the end of the Quran, called the Expansion, or the Opening Up. Tradition says it came to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at a hard time.

It opens with questions: did God not open up your chest, and lift from you the burden that weighed down your back? Before any promise, it remembers relief that has already come. Second, the small word.
Pickthall doesn't write after hardship. He writes with hardship. The ease isn't only waiting at the far end of the road.
It walks alongside the hard thing, already in it, even when it's hard to see. Third, the repeat. Some readers hear it as emphasis, the way a person repeats what matters.
Some commentators go further: they read the twice-said line as one hardship met by two eases. Either way, the chapter won't say its reassurance only once. Fourth, what comes after.
The chapter doesn't end in comfort and a nap.
Its closing verses turn to work and to God: when you're free of one task, keep at the next, and turn your longing to your Lord.
Ease, in this reading, isn't escape from life. It's what makes it possible to keep going inside it.

how: Muslims may recite this chapter in prayer, and some say its line about hardship and ease to one another in difficult times.

o: an Arabic greeting used when a guest arrives
a hadith about the Prophet's hunger in Mecca
a Quran line said twice: ease comes with hardship

games.q: what's inside the chapter — tap the pairs.

s: the line about hardship and ease appears only once in the chapter
it's said twice, back to back.
Pickthall's English says the ease comes with hardship
the chapter ends by telling the listener to rest from all work
its last verses turn to the next task, and to God.

games.q: you're writing down a promise of comfort for someone in a hard time. you've said it once. what does this chapter do?
o: move on to the next point.
add a warning in case it doesn't come true.
games.why: the Quran says it twice: "with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease." some commentators read the repeat as two eases for one hardship.

practice: Hold one hardship you're carrying, and let it be there without arguing with it. Then look inside it, not after it, for one small ease that's with you: a person who checks in, a warm meal, a moment when the worry went quiet.
Rest on the ease for a few breaths, then the hardship, then the ease again; both are here.

wordCard.voice: With hardship: the opening of a line the Quran says twice, with hardship goeth ease. With, not after. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, Quran 94:6: truly, with hardship is ease. 'usr is hardship; yusr is ease.

carryVoice: Your line: it walks alongside. The ease comes with the hardship, not only after it. See you tomorrow.
